overview: Ahold Delhaize is a Dutch-Belgian food retail group formed by the 2016 merger of Royal Ahold (Netherlands) and Delhaize Group (Belgium), operating a portfolio of locally-managed supermarket banners across the U.S. and Europe rather than a single global brand. It generated EUR 92.4 billion of net sales in FY2025 (57.5% U.S., 42.5% Europe) through roughly 9,551 stores (7,199 company-operated, 2,352 franchised) plus the bol.com e-commerce marketplace, and reported a 4.0% underlying operating margin, in line with the low-margin, high-volume, capital-intensive economics typical of grocery retail. The stock trades on Euronext Amsterdam in EUR while the majority of revenue and profit is generated in USD, making the EUR/USD rate a first-order driver of reported (though not underlying local-currency) results.

business_model.summary: Ahold Delhaize earns money by operating supermarkets, pharmacies and an online grocery/marketplace business under a portfolio of strong local banners rather than one global brand. Revenue is overwhelmingly transactional (grocery baskets purchased in-store or online) rather than subscription-based, though loyalty programs, private label, and a growing 'complementary income streams' business (retail media, wholesale/franchise fees, financial services, bol.com marketplace commissions) add higher-margin, quasi-recurring revenue on top of the core low-margin grocery transaction. Segments are reported as 'The United States' and 'Europe' (Europe & Indonesia); the company also breaks out an increasingly important e-commerce channel that reached profitability on a fully allocated basis in H1 2025.

revenue_streams.name: The United States (Food Lion, Stop & Shop, Giant Food, Hannaford, The GIANT Company, FreshDirect)
revenue_streams.trend: stable/slowing (2.0% local-currency growth FY2025, SNAP/pharmacy headwinds in 2026)

revenue_streams.name: Europe (Albert Heijn, Delhaize Belgium, bol.com, Alfa Beta Greece, Mega Image/Profi Romania, Delhaize Serbia, Albert Czech Republic)
revenue_streams.trend: growing (11.7% local-currency growth FY2025, boosted by the Profi acquisition)

revenue_streams.name: Online/e-commerce (grocery + bol.com marketplace, embedded within both segments)
revenue_streams.trend: growing double digits (EUR 10.3bn online sales FY2025, +13.3% constant currency; Q2 2026 +8.6% cc)

revenue_streams.name: Complementary income streams (retail media, wholesale/franchise, financial services, data monetization)
revenue_streams.trend: growing - targeted to reach ~EUR 3bn by 2028 under Growing Together

business_model.customer_type: Primarily B2C mass-market grocery shoppers; some B2B via Albert Heijn's growing B2B delivery service, bol.com's third-party marketplace sellers, and franchise/affiliate store operators (Delhaize Belgium affiliates, ~2,352 franchised stores in Netherlands/Belgium/Luxembourg/Greece)
business_model.geographic_mix: United States 57.5% of net sales / 61.6% of underlying operating income (FY2025); Europe & Indonesia 42.5% of net sales / 38.4% of underlying operating income. Within Europe: Netherlands (Albert Heijn, bol.com), Belgium (Delhaize), Greece (Alfa Beta), Romania (Mega Image + Profi, combined ~2,700 stores across 800+ towns/cities post-acquisition), Serbia, and Czech Republic (Albert).

competitive_position.market_position: Regional/local market leader in most of its footprint rather than a single national #1: Albert Heijn is the clear #1 grocer in the Netherlands with 38.2% market share (up from 37.7% in 2024, outpacing the market for a 7th consecutive year); Food Lion has posted 53 consecutive quarters of positive comparable sales; Hannaford 18 straight quarters. Stop & Shop is the notable laggard, undergoing a multi-year price/format turnaround after admitted value-proposition weakness. bol.com is a top-3 online marketplace in the Netherlands/Belgium. Group-wide, Ahold Delhaize is roughly the 3rd-4th largest food retailer in the U.S. Northeast/Mid-Atlantic and Southeast (via its combined banners) and a top-3 player across its core European markets.

moat_factors.description: Multi-decade store networks (7,199 owned/operated stores) give distribution and logistics density advantages within specific regional footprints (Northeast/Mid-Atlantic and Southeast U.S.; Benelux, Greece, Romania, Serbia, Czech Republic), lowering per-store delivery and supply-chain cost versus new entrants, though this is a regional rather than national moat.

Own-brand penetration exceeded 40% at group level in Q2 2026 (each European brand now carries 900+ 'Price Favorite' own-label products); own brand supports both margin and price-competitiveness versus discounters, and is a core lever of the 'Save for Our Customers' cost program (EUR 1,294m of savings realized in FY2025, cumulative ambition raised to EUR 5bn through 2028).

Digital loyalty programs (bonuskaart at Albert Heijn, U.S. banner loyalty apps) and the proprietary PRISM e-commerce platform (now live across all U.S. banners, serving 26 million weekly customers) generate first-party data used for personalized promotions and are being monetized directly through a nascent retail media business, targeted to help reach ~30 million monthly active digital users and ~80% omnichannel loyalty penetration by 2028.

Decades-old, geographically entrenched local banners (Albert Heijn since 1887, Food Lion, Hannaford) carry strong regional brand equity and customer trust, evidenced by market-share gains and NPS improvement, but this is fragmented across many banners rather than one scalable global brand.

Joint sourcing alliances (e.g., Eurelec purchasing alliance in Europe) and group-wide vendor allowance optimization support gross margin defense (26.5% gross margin FY2025, roughly flat YoY despite price investment), but food retail is fundamentally a low fixed-margin, thin-moat business relative to software or platform models.

weaknesses: Structurally thin margins (~4% underlying operating margin group-wide; grocery is a scale/volume business with limited pricing power against price-transparent discounters)

Stop & Shop remains a structural underperformer requiring ongoing store closures (32 stores closed by end-2024, additional NY/NJ/CT closures confirmed through 2026) and a $1bn multi-year price investment across U.S. banners
Heavily unionized U.S. workforce (UFCW at Stop & Shop and other banners) creates labor cost inflexibility and periodic strike/labor-disruption risk

Fragmented multi-banner structure in Europe (six-plus distinct brands across six countries) limits scale economies relative to a single pan-European operator and complicates cross-border synergy capture
Discounters (Aldi 5.9% and rising, Lidl ~10.6% share in Netherlands) are gaining share structurally in Europe and increasingly compete on Ahold Delhaize's home turf on price and format

growth_drivers: Growing Together strategy (launched 2024, running through 2028): targets ~4% net sales CAGR outperforming the traditional grocery market, industry-leading ~4% average underlying operating margin, cumulative Save for Our Customers savings raised to EUR 5bn, gross CapEx cadence of ~3% of net sales

Complementary income streams (retail media/Ahold Delhaize Media Network, wholesale, franchise, financial services, data monetization) targeted to grow to ~EUR 3 billion by 2028 - a higher-margin overlay on the core grocery business

Online/omnichannel densification: EUR 10.3bn online sales in FY2025 (+13.3% cc), U.S. online +14.5% cc in Q2 2026 marking the 9th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth; e-commerce reached fully-allocated profitability in H1 2025; target of 30 million monthly active digital users and >80% omnichannel loyalty penetration by 2028
Own-brand/private-label expansion (>40% group penetration) supporting both margin and customer value perception amid price-sensitive environment

M&A / bolt-on consolidation: the ~EUR 1.3 billion enterprise value Profi Rom Food acquisition (completed January 2025, ~1,700 stores, ~EUR 2.7-3bn incremental annual sales) doubled Ahold Delhaize's Romanian footprint alongside Mega Image, illustrating continued appetite for regional bolt-on scale deals in fragmented European markets

Continued elevated capital investment (~EUR 2.7 billion gross CapEx guided for FY2026, up from EUR 2.6bn in FY2025) funding new stores, remodels (200+ U.S. remodels, 274 European remodels in FY2025), fulfillment automation, and the PRISM digital platform now live across all U.S. banners

Capital returns: EUR 1 billion share buyback program guided again for 2026 (matching FY2025's completed EUR 1bn buyback) plus a dividend policy targeting 40-50% payout ratio and year-over-year dividend per share growth (EUR 1.24 per share in FY2025, +6.0%)

Potential bol.com subsidiary IPO / value-unlock optionality - management has signaled an 'open mind' to exploring a partial listing of bol.com to crystallize its standalone value, though a prior 2022 IPO attempt was shelved and no transaction has been completed as of Q2 2026

business.risk: U.S. grocery price competition from Walmart, Amazon, discounters and warehouse clubs
business.description: Walmart's scale pricing and Amazon's logistics/Prime ecosystem continue to pressure U.S. banner comparable sales and margins; Ahold Delhaize USA is committing $1 billion over four years to strategic price reductions across its banners specifically to defend share, which will weigh on near-term U.S. margins (U.S. underlying operating margin already declined 0.2pp YoY to 4.2% in Q2 2026).

Stop & Shop's value proposition and pricing were explicitly described by Ahold Delhaize USA's CEO as 'simply not strong enough'; the banner has closed 32 stores (2024) plus additional 2026 closures (Basking Ridge/Westfield NJ, Clinton CT, Toms River NJ) and is mid-turnaround with price cuts across 137 NY/NJ stores in Q2 2026 alone - continued underperformance would be a direct drag on U.S. segment margin and could necessitate further impairments (U.S. banners already booked store-level impairment charges in Q2 2026).

Aldi grew Dutch market share from 5.3% to 5.9% and Lidl holds ~10.6%, structurally eroding the addressable market for full-service grocers like Albert Heijn and Delhaize even as Albert Heijn continues to outgrow the overall market.

FY2025 results cite a Serbian government price-control decree limiting prices and the regulatory cessation of tobacco sales in the Netherlands and Belgium as direct headwinds to European sales and margin.

Integration of the ~EUR 1.3bn Profi acquisition in Romania is still being absorbed (a later-than-expected acquisition close delayed synergy capture and pressured CSE margins in FY2025), and the company had to agree to divest 87 Romanian stores as a post-closing antitrust obligation.

financial.description: The majority of revenue and profit is generated in the U.S. and reported in USD, then translated into EUR for consolidated (and EUR-quoted) results; the USD depreciated 3.98% against the EUR on average in FY2025, which mechanically dampened reported (actual-rate) sales and EPS growth (FY2025 net sales +5.9% at constant rates but only +3.4% at actual rates; diluted underlying EPS +7.8% cc vs +5.0% actual) - a further dollar slide would continue to compress EUR-reported results even if U.S. operations perform in line with local-currency guidance.

financial.risk: Net debt and lease-heavy balance sheet
financial.description: Net debt stood at EUR 14.7 billion at FY2025 year-end (up EUR 570m YoY, driven by the Profi acquisition, dividends and the buyback), of which EUR 10.5 billion is lease liabilities; total gross debt of EUR 18.4 billion. A ratings downgrade below BBB (S&P) / Baa2 (Moody's) would trigger a maximum 5.5x leverage covenant test on the EUR 1.5bn revolving credit facility.

financial.risk: Interest rate sensitivity on insurance/pension liabilities
financial.description: Declining U.S. Treasury yields (3-year yield fell from 4.22% to 3.55% in 2025) increased the present value of insurance liabilities, a modest but recurring financial-statement sensitivity.

regulatory.risk: SNAP (food-stamp) program changes in the U.S.
regulatory.description: SNAP represents roughly 5.3% of Ahold Delhaize's U.S. sales; new SNAP work requirements (effective March 2026, fully enforced from June 2026) contributed to enrollment falling by over 5.3 million people year-over-year as of April 2026, cutting U.S. sales growth by ~40 basis points in Q2 2026 and an expected 60-80bps drag for full-year 2026.

regulatory.risk: U.S. pharmacy pricing / Inflation Reduction Act
regulatory.description: IRA-related pharmacy pricing changes reduced U.S. comparable sales growth by 0.7 percentage points in Q2 2026, a direct and ongoing regulatory margin/revenue headwind in the pharmacy counters embedded within U.S. supermarkets.

Romanian competition clearance for the Profi deal required divestiture of 87 stores, illustrating that further consolidation in concentrated local markets (Netherlands, Belgium, Romania) may face regulatory constraints.

Stop & Shop's historical withdrawal from the UFCW-Industry Pension Fund carried an after-tax cost of roughly $500 million paid in installments, and Giant Food separately recorded an ~$800 million pension-related liability from the FELRA/MAP multiemployer plan settlement; while these are largely resolved/de-risked, residual multi-employer plan exposure and any future underfunding at plans the company still participates in remain a tail risk given heavy UFCW unionization across U.S. banners.

macro.description: Sharp deflation in egg prices was specifically cited as a Q2 2026 headwind to U.S. comparable sales; conversely, tariff-driven input cost inflation could reverse this dynamic and pressure margins if not fully passed through to shelf prices.

As a large importer of private-label and general merchandise goods (particularly through bol.com's marketplace and U.S. non-food categories), U.S. tariff policy changes raise input costs that the company may only partially pass on to price-sensitive consumers without ceding further share to discounters.

Management has repeatedly cited a 'persistent macroeconomic and geopolitical' backdrop and reduced consumer spending power in Central/Southeast Europe as pressuring both volumes and margins across FY2025 and into 2026.

execution.description: President & CEO Frans Muller, in the role since July 2018, is set to retire around the April 2027 AGM; the Supervisory Board has nominated Thierry Garnier (former Kingfisher plc CEO) as his successor. Leadership transitions at large multi-banner retailers carry execution risk around strategic continuity, and the transition coincides with the separate departure of Claude Sarrailh, CEO of Ahold Delhaize Europe & Indonesia, who is leaving to become CEO of Esselunga.

Management's stated openness to a bol.com subsidiary IPO (after shelving a prior 2022 attempt) creates ongoing uncertainty about the eventual ownership structure and capital allocation of one of the group's fastest-growing digital assets.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global grocery retail is a large but low-growth, low-margin, highly competitive industry (typical operating margins of 3-5%); the IMF projects 1.4% real GDP growth in Europe for 2026 (in line with 1.3% in 2025) with 2.8% average consumer price inflation, moderating from prior years. U.S. grocery growth is being reshaped by continued discounter/warehouse club share gains, e-commerce penetration (still under 10% of U.S. grocery spend but growing double digits), and policy shifts (SNAP, IRA pharmacy pricing, tariffs).
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-moderate - food retail is a defensive consumer staple with resilient volumes through economic cycles, but comparable sales growth, mix (trade-down to private label/discounters), and government transfer programs (SNAP) are sensitive to consumer disposable income and unemployment.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - a highly leveraged, capital-intensive balance sheet (EUR 18.4bn gross debt, EUR 10.5bn of which is lease liabilities) means financing costs and the present value of insurance/pension liabilities are rate-sensitive; net financial expense rose 15.2% YoY in FY2025 partly on higher interest costs from Profi-related lease liabilities.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: High and structural - the majority of group revenue and profit is USD-denominated (U.S. segment = 57.5% of net sales) while the company reports and is quoted in EUR; USD depreciated 3.98% against EUR on average in FY2025, meaningfully dampening EUR-reported (actual-rate) growth versus constant-currency growth in both sales and EPS. Secondary exposure to RON, CZK and RSD in Central/Southeast Europe.
key_input_costs: Food commodity costs (produce, dairy, eggs, meat)
Labor (heavily unionized U.S. workforce, minimum wage inflation)
Tariff-exposed imported general merchandise (notably via bol.com)

recent_developments.event: Q2 2026 results: net sales EUR 23.2bn (+1.9% cc, +0.3% actual); comparable sales ex-gas +1.2% group (U.S. +0.8%, Europe +1.7%); underlying operating margin 3.9% (-0.1pt cc); diluted underlying EPS EUR 0.63 (-1.4% cc); online sales +8.6% cc (U.S. +14.5% cc, 9th straight quarter of double-digit U.S. online growth); FY2026 guidance reiterated.

Management disclosed SNAP benefit reductions cut U.S. sales growth by ~40bps in Q2 2026 with an expected 60-80bps full-year drag, and IRA pharmacy pricing changes cut U.S. comparable sales by 0.7pp; Stop & Shop cut prices across 137 NY/NJ stores and Albert Heijn cut prices on 500+ 'Price Favorite' items.

Additional confirmed Stop & Shop store closures for 2026 (Basking Ridge and Westfield, NJ; Clinton, CT in October 2026; Toms River, NJ in late spring 2026), continuing the post-2024 (32-store) turnaround/rationalization of the underperforming banner.

Ahold Delhaize's Supervisory Board nominated Thierry Garnier, former CEO of Kingfisher plc, as President & CEO-designate; incumbent Frans Muller (CEO since July 2018) will retire around the April 2027 AGM. Separately, Claude Sarrailh, CEO of Ahold Delhaize Europe & Indonesia, resigned to become CEO of Italian retailer Esselunga.
Q1 2026 results showed continued double-digit U.S. online growth but flagged SNAP and macro headwinds; management maintained FY2026 guidance.

Q4/FY2025 results: net sales EUR 92.4bn (+5.9% cc, +3.4% actual); underlying operating margin 4.0% (flat YoY, in line with ~4% target); diluted underlying EPS EUR 2.67 (+7.8% cc, +5.0% actual); free cash flow EUR 2.6bn (target was 'at least EUR 2.2bn'); net income EUR 2.264bn (+28.4%); EUR 1 billion share buyback completed; dividend per share EUR 1.24 (+6.0%, 47% payout ratio); FY2026 guidance issued (underlying operating margin ~4%, FCF at least EUR 2.3bn, gross CapEx ~EUR 2.7bn, mid-to-high-single-digit underlying EPS growth cc, new EUR 1bn buyback and dividend growth intent).

Completed the ~EUR 1.3 billion enterprise-value acquisition of Profi Rom Food SRL (~1,700 Romanian stores) from MidEuropa, roughly doubling the group's Romanian retail footprint alongside Mega Image; subsequently agreed to divest 87 stores to Annabella as a competition-clearance condition.

bol.com strategic-review optionality remains live; management has publicly kept the door open to a subsidiary IPO of bol.com after the 2022 IPO attempt was shelved, without committing to a timeline or transaction as of the Q2 2026 report.

items.notes: Reiterated at Q2 2026 after Q2 actual underlying operating margin came in at 3.9% (down 0.1pt cc), with European improvement offset by a modest U.S. decline (U.S. underlying operating margin 4.2%, down 0.2pt vs LY).

items.target: mid- to high-single-digit growth, at constant exchange rates
items.notes: Q2 2026 diluted underlying EPS was EUR 0.63, down 1.4% cc year-over-year, meaning H2 2026 needs to accelerate materially to hit the full-year target; FY2025 underlying EPS grew 7.8% cc.

items.vs_prior: maintained (raised versus FY2025's original EUR 2.2bn target; FY2025 actual was EUR 2.6bn)
items.notes: H1 2026 FCF was EUR 302m, down from EUR 715m in H1 2025, reflecting calendar/seasonal phasing per company commentary; full-year target excludes M&A.

items.vs_prior: raised vs. FY2025 actual of EUR 2.6 billion (FY2025 target was also ~EUR 2.7bn)
items.notes: Funds store openings/remodels, digital/omnichannel infrastructure (PRISM), fulfillment automation and supply-chain modernization.

items.vs_prior: raised vs. FY2025 actual of EUR 1.294 billion (which itself was slightly down from EUR 1.354bn in FY2024)
items.notes: Part of the cumulative EUR 5 billion savings ambition through 2028 under the Growing Together strategy.

items.vs_prior: maintained (same size as the completed FY2025 buyback)
items.notes: Management states buyback and dividend programs remain subject to ongoing assessment of macroeconomic, geopolitical and legislative factors, and may be adjusted for M&A activity.
FY2025 interim dividend was EUR 0.51 (matched in the FY2026 interim dividend); FY2025 full-year DPS was EUR 1.24 (+6.0%) at a 47% payout ratio.

items.target: ~4% net sales CAGR outperforming the market; ~4% average underlying operating margin; cumulative EUR 5bn Save for Our Customers savings; ~3% of net sales gross CapEx cadence; ~EUR 3bn complementary income streams; >80% omnichannel loyalty penetration; 30 million monthly active digital users
items.vs_prior: n/a (medium-term strategy framework, unchanged since 2024 launch)
items.notes: These multi-year targets, not single-year guidance, underpin the FY2026 annual guidance figures above.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Frans Muller characterized Q2 2026 as a 'resilient performance' achieved through 'disciplined investments in customer value propositions, innovation and growth, combined with strong cost management,' citing market-share gains across major markets and brands 'in an uncertain macroeconomic environment.' Management explicitly flagged SNAP benefit cuts, IRA pharmacy pricing, and egg-price deflation as U.S. headwinds, and reiterated full FY2026 guidance despite Q2 underlying EPS declining 1.4% at constant currency, implying confidence in H2 2026 acceleration (Save for Our Customers savings, Profi synergy ramp, and continued price/cost discipline).

bull_case: Growing Together strategy is tracking to target: FY2025 delivered 5.9% constant-currency sales growth, a 4.0% underlying operating margin (in line with the ~4% multi-year target), and 7.8% constant-currency underlying EPS growth, evidencing execution credibility ahead of the 2028 targets (4% CAGR, EUR 5bn cumulative savings, EUR 3bn complementary income by 2028).

Structural online/omnichannel growth with improving unit economics: group online sales reached EUR 10.3bn in FY2025 (+13.3% cc) and e-commerce turned profitable on a fully allocated basis in H1 2025; U.S. online growth has now posted nine consecutive quarters of double-digit growth (+14.5% cc in Q2 2026), and the PRISM platform rollout across all U.S. banners should support further margin improvement in digital.

Consistent, growing shareholder capital returns: a EUR 1 billion share buyback completed in FY2025 and another EUR 1bn guided for FY2026, alongside a dividend raised 6.0% to EUR 1.24/share (47% payout ratio, within the 40-50% policy range), on top of a resilient EUR 2.6bn FY2025 free cash flow (target of at least EUR 2.3bn for FY2026) that comfortably covers both.

Market-share momentum in core banners despite discounter pressure: Albert Heijn gained Dutch market share for a seventh consecutive year (38.2%, from 37.7%), Food Lion posted 53 consecutive quarters of positive comparable sales, and Hannaford 18 consecutive quarters - evidence that scale, private label (>40% group penetration) and loyalty/personalization are defending share even against Aldi/Lidl and Walmart/Amazon.

Optionality on bol.com: management's continued openness to a subsidiary IPO of the fast-growing Dutch/Belgian e-commerce marketplace represents a potential value-crystallization catalyst not currently reflected in the consolidated grocery-retailer multiple the stock trades at (12-month analyst price targets average roughly EUR 38-40 versus an August 2026 share price around EUR 31, implying meaningful analyst-perceived upside).
bear_case: Stop & Shop remains a genuine drag with no clear end date: the banner needed 32 store closures by end-2024 plus further 2026 closures (NJ, CT locations), a $1bn multi-year U.S. price-investment program, and Q2 2026 impairment charges on operating stores - continued underperformance directly weighs on the U.S. segment, which still generates 61.6% of group underlying operating income.

Currency is a persistent, uncontrollable drag on EUR-reported results: with 57.5% of sales USD-denominated against a EUR-quoted, EUR-reporting entity, a 3.98% average USD depreciation in FY2025 alone cut reported net sales growth from 5.9% (constant currency) to 3.4% (actual), and diluted underlying EPS growth from 7.8% to 5.0% - further dollar weakness would continue eroding headline EUR results even amid solid underlying operational execution.

U.S. policy and pricing headwinds are compounding, not one-off: SNAP eligibility changes (5.3+ million fewer enrollees YoY as of April 2026, ~5.3% of U.S. sales at risk, 60-80bps FY2026 sales drag), IRA pharmacy pricing pressure (-0.7pp on Q2 2026 U.S. comparable sales), and egg-price deflation collectively show a U.S. business facing simultaneous top-line and margin pressure that management is only partially offsetting with cost savings, evidenced by Q2 2026 U.S. underlying operating margin declining 0.2pt YoY to 4.2% and group underlying EPS falling 1.4% cc in the quarter despite reiterated full-year guidance.

Structurally thin, hard-to-expand margins in a discounter-pressured market: group underlying operating margin has been flat at 4.0% for two straight years despite the Growing Together program, discounters (Aldi, Lidl) continue taking European share, and the FY2026 guide of 'around 4%' embeds no meaningful margin expansion - meaning EPS growth depends almost entirely on sales growth, cost-cutting, and buybacks rather than structural margin re-rating.

Leadership transition and unresolved corporate-structure questions add execution uncertainty: CEO Frans Muller's planned 2027 retirement and incoming CEO Thierry Garnier's lack of grocery-sector (versus home-improvement) experience, combined with the departure of the Europe & Indonesia CEO and the still-undecided fate of bol.com (an unresolved strategic overhang since the shelved 2022 IPO), create governance and strategic-continuity risk at a company already carrying EUR 14.7bn of net debt.
